obs_1: **Fee drag** : The yearly slice your investments pay in fees adds up, over the full span of retirement, to a sum that would cover years of your monthly income. Because that cost compounds silently season after season, it is the single largest leak you have the power to seal, and a leaner fee structure could redirect much of it back into your own pocket.
obs_2: **Forced withdrawals** : Once your registered savings convert to a Registered Retirement Income Fund, the minimum you must withdraw climbs as a share of the balance with every passing year. Because so much of your wealth is registered, that rising floor could steer your taxable income upward in your later years regardless of what you actually want to spend.
obs_3: **Estate tax split** : The money left in your registered account is fully taxable in the year of death, while your tax-free savings pass to your heirs without any tax at all. That difference means the order in which you spend these accounts during your lifetime could quietly reshape how much of your estate survives the final tax bill.
obs_4: **Supplement floor** : Once your Canada Pension Plan and Old Age Security are flowing, your guaranteed income also includes the Guaranteed Income Supplement, and together these sources carry your planned spending in full. Because this is a supplement-eligible profile, the way you draw from your savings could affect how much of that supplement you keep, since added taxable income can reduce it.
obs_5: **Floor over portfolio** : Your personal savings are slim, yet your guaranteed government income already shoulders your whole spending target, which flips the usual worry on its head. That means your portfolio's real job is flexibility for surprises rather than survival, so a registered withdrawal that nudges your taxable income could cost you more in lost supplement than it gains you in spending.
next_horizon: The data suggests the most useful window ahead lies in trimming fees and keeping an eye on how any withdrawal could affect your income-tested supplement, rather than in drawing your registered savings down faster.
